name: Western Honeybee
description: The world's most famous bee! Lives in colonies of up to 80,000 and produces the honey we eat.
habitat: Worldwide (managed hives and wild colonies)
diet: Nectar and pollen from a wide variety of flowers
funFact: A single honeybee visits 50-100 flowers per trip and must visit about 2 million flowers to make one pound of honey.
culturalNote: Ancient Egyptians believed bees were born from the tears of the sun god Ra.
superpower: Waggle Dance GPS — communicates exact flower locations through dance!

name: Common Bumblebee
description: Big, fuzzy, and loud! Bumblebees are the heavyweight champions of pollination with their signature buzz.
habitat: Meadows, gardens, forests across Europe and temperate regions
diet: Nectar and pollen, especially from clover, foxglove, and lavender
funFact: Bumblebees can vibrate their flight muscles at middle C to shake pollen loose — it's called 'buzz pollination' and honeybees can't do it!
culturalNote: Scientists once said bumblebees shouldn't be able to fly based on aerodynamics — they were wrong!
superpower: Buzz Pollination — vibrates at 130 Hz to shake loose pollen that other bees can't reach!

name: Blue Orchard Mason Bee
description: A solitary superstar! Just 250 mason bees can do the pollination work of 30,000 honeybees.
habitat: Orchards, gardens, woodland edges across North America
diet: Pollen and nectar from fruit trees and spring wildflowers
funFact: Mason bees are 120x more efficient at pollinating than honeybees because they're so messy — pollen goes everywhere!
culturalNote: Native Americans observed these bees as early signs of spring and fruit season.
superpower: Super Pollinator — 120x more efficient than honeybees!

name: Eastern Carpenter Bee
description: These chunky bees look scary but are gentle giants. They drill perfectly round holes in wood to build their nests.
habitat: Wooden structures, dead trees, fence posts across eastern North America
diet: Nectar from open-faced flowers, especially wisteria and passion flowers
funFact: Male carpenter bees hover aggressively near their nest but they have no stinger — it's all bluff!
culturalNote: Carpenter bees have been building in human structures for thousands of years — some consider them nature's carpenters.
superpower: Power Drill — chews perfectly round tunnels through solid wood!

name: Metallic Green Sweat Bee
description: Tiny, shimmering emerald jewels of the bee world. They're attracted to human sweat for the salt!
habitat: Gardens, meadows, and fields across the Americas
diet: Nectar and pollen from small wildflowers, daisies, and sunflowers
funFact: Some sweat bees can navigate by starlight — they're one of the few insects known to fly at night using the Milky Way!
culturalNote: Their metallic green color comes from light refracting off layered structures in their exoskeleton, like a living prism.
superpower: Starlight Navigation — can fly at night using the Milky Way!

name: Alfalfa Leafcutter Bee
description: Nature's crafters! They cut perfect circles from leaves to build cozy nest cells for their babies.
habitat: Agricultural areas, gardens, meadows worldwide
diet: Pollen from alfalfa, clover, and wildflowers
funFact: Leafcutter bees carry pollen on their bellies instead of their legs — they belly-flop onto flowers!
culturalNote: Farmers deliberately use leafcutter bees to pollinate alfalfa crops — they're worth millions to agriculture.
superpower: Belly Pollen — carries pollen on their fuzzy stomach for maximum flower contact!

name: Golden Orchid Bee
description: Iridescent flying jewels! Males collect perfumes from orchids to attract mates in the most fabulous courtship in nature.
habitat: Tropical forests of Central and South America, recently southern Florida
diet: Nectar from orchids and tropical flowers
funFact: Male orchid bees have special pouches on their back legs where they store a custom perfume blend collected from up to 10 different orchid species!
culturalNote: Indigenous peoples of the Amazon have long associated these iridescent bees with forest spirits.
superpower: Perfume Collector — creates a custom cologne from orchid scents to attract a mate!

name: Nomad Cuckoo Bee
description: The bee world's sneakiest villain! Cuckoo bees lay their eggs in other bees' nests, like the cuckoo bird.
habitat: Wherever their host bees live — meadows, gardens, woodland edges
diet: Steals pollen provisions from host bee nests
funFact: Cuckoo bees have no pollen-collecting hairs because they never need to gather pollen — they let other bees do the work!
culturalNote: Like the cuckoo bird they're named after, these bees are 'brood parasites' — a survival strategy that's existed for millions of years.
superpower: Master of Disguise — mimics the scent of host bees to sneak past defenses!

name: Giant Honeybee
description: Builds massive exposed combs on cliffs and tall trees. Famous for their 'Mexican wave' defense!
habitat: Tropical forests and cliffs of South and Southeast Asia
diet: Nectar and pollen from tropical flowering trees
funFact: When threatened, thousands of bees do a synchronized 'shimmering' wave across the nest surface — it scares away predators like a stadium wave!
culturalNote: Honey hunters in Nepal and India climb cliffs to harvest their honey — a tradition thousands of years old.
superpower: Shimmer Wave — coordinates thousands of bees in a synchronized defense display!

name: Maya Stingless Bee
description: Sacred to the ancient Maya! These gentle, stingless bees produce a rare medicinal honey prized for centuries.
habitat: Tropical forests of Mexico and Central America
diet: Nectar from tropical flowers, fruits, and tree resins
funFact: Their honey is thinner and tangier than regular honey and has been used as medicine for wound healing for over 3,000 years!
culturalNote: The Maya worshipped a stingless bee god called Ah Muzen Cab and kept these bees in special log hives for centuries.
superpower: Sacred Honey — produces rare medicinal honey used for healing since ancient Maya times!

name: Tawny Mining Bee
description: Fuzzy orange diggers that build underground nests! You might spot their mini volcano-shaped nest entrances in your lawn.
habitat: Gardens, lawns, parks, and paths across Europe
diet: Pollen from fruit trees, dandelions, and spring wildflowers
funFact: Mining bees create tiny volcano-shaped mounds of soil at their nest entrance — like mini ant hills but for bees!
culturalNote: In Britain, the appearance of tawny mining bees is a beloved sign of spring.
superpower: Earth Mover — excavates underground tunnels with multiple nursery chambers!

name: European Wool Carder Bee
description: Scrapes fuzzy fibers from plant leaves to build the softest, coziest bee nests in nature.
habitat: Gardens with lamb's ear, foxglove, and other fuzzy-leaved plants
diet: Nectar from tubular flowers like foxglove and snapdragons
funFact: Males are fiercely territorial — they body-slam other insects (even bumblebees!) to defend their favorite flower patch.
culturalNote: Named 'wool carder' because they comb plant fibers like a person carding wool for spinning.
superpower: Body Slam — males tackle intruders mid-air to defend their territory!

name: Long-Horned Bee
description: Males sport ridiculously long antennae — sometimes longer than their entire body!
habitat: Meadows, grasslands, and coastal areas of Europe
diet: Specialist — only collects pollen from plants in the pea family
funFact: Their absurdly long antennae help males detect female pheromones from far away — like having a built-in satellite dish!
culturalNote: These bees are indicator species — when they disappear, it means wildflower meadows are in trouble.
superpower: Mega Antennae — detects mates from incredible distances with oversized sensors!

name: Blue-Banded Bee
description: Australia's most beautiful bee! Brilliant turquoise stripes and an incredible buzz pollination technique.
habitat: Gardens, forests, and urban areas across Australia and Southeast Asia
diet: Nectar from tomatoes, eggplants, and native Australian flowers
funFact: Blue-banded bees head-bang flowers at 350 times per second to release pollen — they're the heavy metal stars of the bee world!
culturalNote: Indigenous Australians have observed these bees for thousands of years and associate them with healthy Country.
superpower: Head-Banger — vibrates flowers at 350 Hz by literally headbutting them!

name: Rusty Patched Bumblebee
description: Once common across eastern North America, now critically endangered. One of the first bees listed under the Endangered Species Act.
habitat: Grasslands, prairies, and open woodlands (historically widespread, now extremely rare)
diet: Pollen from wildflowers, clover, and native prairie plants
funFact: This bee's population has declined by 87% since the late 1990s — but conservation efforts are slowly bringing them back in some areas!
culturalNote: The rusty patched bumblebee became a symbol of the pollinator conservation movement in the US.
superpower: Survivor Spirit — fighting back from the edge of extinction with human help!

name: Teddy Bear Bee
description: Round, golden, and impossibly fuzzy — they look exactly like tiny flying teddy bears!
habitat: Gardens, parks, and eucalyptus forests of eastern Australia
diet: Nectar from lavender, abelia, and native Australian plants
funFact: Teddy bear bees sleep by clamping their jaws onto a plant stem and hanging there all night — sometimes in groups, like a bee sleepover!
culturalNote: These bees have become social media stars in Australia — their cute appearance helps people care about native pollinators.
superpower: Hang Time — sleeps by dangling from stems with its jaw, sometimes in adorable groups!

name: Alkali Bee
description: These ground-nesting bees are alfalfa pollination champions — farmers create special bee beds for them!
habitat: Alkali soil flats near agricultural areas in western North America
diet: Specialist on alfalfa, also visits sunflowers and other crops
funFact: Farmers build special 'bee beds' — maintained patches of alkaline soil — to attract millions of these bees for crop pollination!
culturalNote: The relationship between alkali bees and alfalfa farmers is one of the best examples of humans and native bees working together.
superpower: Farm Partner — teams up with humans in specially built bee beds for massive pollination!

name: Vulture Bee
description: The only bees in the world that eat MEAT! They evolved to feed on animal carcasses instead of flowers.
habitat: Tropical forests of Central and South America
diet: Rotting meat (yes, really!) — they produce a honey-like substance from it
funFact: Vulture bees have an extra tooth on their mandibles for cutting meat, and their gut microbiome is more like a vulture's than a bee's!
culturalNote: Despite eating meat, vulture bees produce a sweet, edible substance from their protein diet — indigenous peoples have tasted it for centuries.
superpower: Carnivore — the only bees on Earth that eat meat instead of pollen!

name: Himalayan Giant Honeybee
description: The world's largest honeybee! Builds massive combs on Himalayan cliff faces and produces the legendary 'mad honey.'
habitat: Himalayan cliffs at 2,500-3,500m altitude in Nepal, Bhutan, and India
diet: Nectar from rhododendrons and alpine wildflowers
funFact: Their honey from rhododendron nectar contains grayanotoxin — it's called 'mad honey' because it causes hallucinations! Honey hunters risk their lives on cliff ladders to harvest it.
culturalNote: The Gurung people of Nepal have harvested this honey for thousands of years using rope ladders on sheer cliff faces — one of humanity's most dangerous traditions.
superpower: Cliff Dweller — nests on sheer Himalayan cliff faces at 3,000+ meters altitude!

name: Neon Cuckoo Bee
description: Electric blue spots on jet black — the most punk rock looking bee on the planet. And yes, it's a nest thief.
habitat: Gardens and bushland of Australia
diet: Steals pollen provisions from blue-banded bee nests
funFact: This bee specifically targets blue-banded bees — it sneaks into their nests while they're out foraging and lays its own eggs!
culturalNote: The neon cuckoo bee is proof that evolution has a sense of style — it's the most photogenic insect in Australia.
superpower: Neon Stealth — its dazzling appearance distracts while it infiltrates host nests!
